title: Diabetic foot care training and the presence of nurses in Turkish YouTube videos
screen_reason: Content analysis of 87 Turkish-language YouTube videos on diabetic foot care with an explicit binary code for “presence of misleading information”: 4.6% of the 87 videos were found to contain misleading information. That is a share of items in a sample coded as misleading, with a stated denominator, so it qualifies as CONTENT. The usefulness/DISCERN/GQS scoring in the same paper is QUALITY and is recorded separately.

estimates.date: search performed 09.12.2020; videos published in the preceding 8 years
estimates.measure_type: % of Turkish YouTube videos on diabetic foot care that contained misleading information
estimates.value_raw: 4.6% were found to contain misleading information (of the n = 87 videos included)
estimates.denominator: 87 Turkish-language YouTube videos retained from the 200 videos returned by the keyword search “diabetic foot care” (exclusions: not related to diabetic foot or its care, no audio, advertising content, repeats, not in Turkish, herbal products)
estimates.definition: Video coded by the two investigators as containing misleading information; the code is recorded as a binary presence/absence alongside video source, content, training method and presence of distractions, and no operational criterion for “misleading” is stated
estimates.misinfo_def: None given; the paper records the “presence of misleading information” without defining what counts as misleading.
estimates.source_quote: Of the videos included in the study based on our inclusion criteria, 4.6% were found to contain misleading information.
estimates.page_loc: p. 432, Results (also in the Abstract: “while 4.6% contained misleading information”) and repeated in the Discussion p. 433
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent investigators (nursing academics at Bursa Uludag University) evaluated each video; inter-investigator agreement of 100% (Kappa 1.00) is reported only for the usefulness classification, and no reliability statistic or coding rule is given for the “misleading information” code
estimates.moderator_quote: A search was performed on YouTube (www.youtube.com) video sharing platform using the keyword "diabetic foot care" on 09.12.2020. A total of 200 videos published in the last 8 years that the search returned were subjected to preliminary examination.
estimates.notes: Rank-truncated set (top 200 search results, first-page-style truncation), hence denom_selection=curated on a single-issue topical denominator. The denominator is heavily filtered: 33 videos were dropped as not related to diabetic foot and 47 as not related to diabetic foot care, and the authors themselves say that including those would have raised the not-useful share. 4.6% of 87 corresponds to 4 videos, but the paper never states the count, so only the verbatim percentage is recorded. The authors contrast their figure with Gimenez-Perez et al., who reported “approximately one quarter” of diabetes videos misleading; that is a cited figure from another study and is not extracted.

estimates.date: search performed 09.12.2020; videos published in the preceding 8 years
estimates.measure_type: % of Turkish YouTube videos on diabetic foot care rated “not useful” on a 15-item diabetic-foot-care content checklist
estimates.value_raw: 6.9% as not useful [full distribution: very useful 7 (8.0%), moderately useful 29 (33.3%), somewhat useful 45 (51.7%), not useful 6 (6.9%)]
estimates.denominator: 87 Turkish-language YouTube videos retained from the 200 returned by the keyword search “diabetic foot care”
estimates.definition: Video scored 0 on a 15-item checklist of diabetic foot care recommendations drawn from leading healthcare organisations (one point per item present); 0 = not useful, 1–5 = somewhat useful, 6–10 = moderately useful, 11+ = very useful
estimates.misinfo_def: None given; the usefulness scale measures completeness of recommended content, not veracity.
estimates.source_quote: Of the 87 videos evaluated, 8% were categorized as very useful, 33.3% moderately useful, 51.7% somewhat useful, and 6.9% as not useful.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two independent investigators applied a 15-item checklist built from guideline sources (APMA, IDF, HRSA, Turkish consensus report); inter-investigator reliability for the usefulness classification was 100% (Kappa score: 1.00); the authors list the subjectivity of the criteria as a limitation
estimates.moderator_quote: Usefulness of the videos included in the study was evaluated according to the 15-item checklist prepared in line with the literature ... One point was given for containing each item. Based on the total score, the videos were divided into 4 categories of usefulness: not useful (0), somewhat useful (1− 5), moderately useful (6− 10), and very useful
estimates.notes: QUALITY, not CONTENT, and excluded from prevalence per §3: a completely accurate video can be scored “not useful” simply for covering none of the 15 recommended items, so the label carries no veracity claim. Recorded as the negative pole of the scale; the full four-category distribution is in value_raw. Note the separate misleading-content code (4.6%) is a different, much smaller quantity, and the two must not be conflated.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) Mean DISCERN reliability 2.68 ± 0.76 (0–5) and mean GQS quality 2.78 ± 0.83 (1–5), plus the per-usefulness-group means in Table 3: scale means with no share of items, so no row per the protocol. (2) Distractions: 27.4% of videos had distracting factors (13.8% video quality, 5.7% background, 4.6% length, 3.3% speaker). Distraction is a presentation attribute, not a veracity or quality-of-information judgement, so no construct applies. (3) Nurse presence: 12.6% of videos had a nurse as speaker, 87.4% did not; a source-attribute share, not a misinformation measure. (4) Table 2 source/content/training-method distributions and Table 4 per-item coverage counts: descriptive composition of the corpus, not misinformation shares. (5) Figures cited from other studies (Abedin et al. 11.2%/14.6%/24.7%/49.4%; Smith et al. 64.4%/35.6%; Silva et al. 6.29%/16.35%/24.35%/52.83%; Gimenez-Perez “approximately one quarter of the videos contained misleading information”): all cited from elsewhere, barred by R8. (6) The count behind 4.6% is never stated; 4.6% of 87 is about 4 videos but the paper gives no numerator, so only the percentage is recorded. JUDGEMENT CALL for the adjudicator: the “misleading information” code is a bare binary with no stated criterion and no reliability statistic (the Kappa 1.00 covers only the usefulness classification), so the CONTENT row rests on an undocumented instrument even though the value itself is unambiguous.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. One keyword search (“diabetic foot care”) run on 09.12.2020, returning 200 videos from the preceding 8 years; videos unrelated to diabetic foot (n = 33) or to diabetic foot care (n = 47), without audio, advertising, repeated, non-Turkish or featuring herbal products were excluded, leaving 87. Each video was rated independently by two investigators for usefulness (15-item checklist derived from healthcare-organisation recommendations), reliability (5 items adapted from DISCERN) and quality (GQS 1–5); reliability and quality scores were averaged across the two raters, and inter-investigator agreement was 100% (Kappa 1.00) for the usefulness classification only. Presence of misleading information and of distractions were recorded as additional binary codes with no stated criteria and no reliability statistic. Analysis: descriptive statistics, chi-square, ANOVA/Kruskal-Wallis in SPSS 23.0. Authors list as limitations that the usefulness criteria and the exclusion criteria were subjective, that only the first 200 videos were screened, and that only one keyword set and only Turkish-language videos were used.
rob.item6_quote: In addition, video source (Professional organization/Hospital/University, TV channel/ Newspaper, professional person, commercial organization, private users, and medical website), content (training, training-TV program, news, people and blogs), training method (plain narration, question-answer, visual support, and demonstration), presence of distractions, and presence of misleading information were recorded.
rob.item10_quote: Of the videos included in the study based on our inclusion criteria, 4.6% were found to contain misleading information.
